newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Buba within target range with June M3 growth.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Buba within target range with June M3 growth.

text.p: German M3 money supply growth moved into the Bundesbank's target zone for the first time this year on Monday, reinforcing expectations for a steady interest rate environment in the coming months.

The M3 measure of money supply, one of the central bank's key policy indicators, grew by 6.4 percent in June compared with the fourth quarter of 1996, significantly lower than the 7.0 percent growth seen in May.
The Bundesbank's target range for M3 in 1997 is 3.5 to 6.5 percent.

"It is very important to see money supply growth coming into the target range so that from this side we have further confirmation that the Bundesbank will not change short-term rates in the foreseeable future," said Juergen Pfister, economist at Commerzbank in Frankfurt.
The 1997 M3 growth target range will come under the microscope at the central bank's regular council meeting on Thursday -- the last before the summer break.
The Bundesbank's record for hitting its target is at best patchy, with annual M3 rates coming within target zones only 50 percent of the time in the last 20 years.
This track record has prompted some calls for the Bundesbank to abandon M3 as a leading indicator for monetary policy and adopt direct inflation targets such as used by the Bank of England.

But the central bank has said it will stay with its pattern of setting an M3 target zone, and analysts say the 3.5 to 6.5 percent spread is unlikely to be altered on Thursday, particularly now that money supply growth has edged inside the upper boundary.
The Bundesbank said June's growth slowdown was a reflection of reduced lending and stronger capital formation, but added that cash in circulation had also increased significantly in June.
"These figures are naturally very good," said Gerhard Grebe, chief economist at Bank Julius Baer in Frankfurt. "The reduced lending and stronger monetary capital formation is very positive."
Capital formation occurs when investors put money in longer-term investments, taking it out of the normal money supply circulation areas counted under the M3 measure.

Analysts said lower levels of lending to the private sector reflected a pick-up in banks' ability to place equity with foreign investors in June, reducing the need for bank credit, while a slowdown in public borrowing was a sign that this sector had turned more to the bond market for funds.
Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International in London, said the fresh M3 data should be supportive for the bond market.
"The key aspect was the slowdown we saw in private sector lending. That has been stuck fairly high recently ... so that is the most encouraging aspect of the figures," he said.
"In addition, we have seen a pick-up in capital formation, which does suggest that German investors have found funds increasingly attractive in June."
German debt prices were nevertheless lower in early dealings on Monday, with the September DTB Bund future trading 14 basis points lower at 102.58 by 0907 GMT.
